messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Joe is a 39-year-old construction worker, divorced for the past four years, who lives alone in a small apartment on the outskirts of town. He came to therapy at the urging of his foreman, who noticed that Joe had become increasingly irritable and withdrawn on the job site, sometimes staring blankly into the middle distance when heavy machinery rumbled nearby. The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, during a routine demolition job. Joe was operating a jackhammer on the second floor of an old warehouse when a support beam gave way above him. He looked up just in time to see a co-worker, a man named Carlos, lose his footing and fall through the collapsing floor, landing on the concrete slab below with a sound Joe still hears in his sleep. Carlos died at the scene. Joe had known him for years.

In the weeks that followed, Joe found himself haunted by the image of Carlos falling, the way his body seemed to hang in the air for a fraction of a second too long. The memory came as vivid pictures, snapshots of that moment that would flash into his mind without warning. What he found most disturbing was the smell—the sharp, metallic tang of dust and hydraulic fluid that had filled the air that day. He would be standing at his workbench, and suddenly he could taste it, the grit of concrete dust on his tongue, as if the event were happening all over again. These sensory intrusions made him feel helpless, and he became certain that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He had always believed that hard work and caution kept danger at bay, but that belief was destroyed. Now he saw the world as a place where catastrophe could strike at any moment, and he was inadequate to prevent it. Because he was convinced that he could not handle the feelings that came with these memories, he began to avoid them. He suppressed his anger, never allowing himself to feel or express it, because he was certain that if he let it out, he would lose control completely. He started gambling online in the evenings, placing small bets on sports games just to distract himself, to feel a flicker of excitement that pushed the images away for a few hours. On the worst nights, when the smell of dust seemed to fill his apartment, he would deliberately try to leave his body, blanking out his mind until the world went fuzzy and distant.

The more Joe tried to suppress his reactions, the more vivid the memories became. He found that the harder he worked to push the images away, the more frequently they returned, each time bringing with them the taste and the smell and the crushing sense of his own inadequacy. He started to believe that the memory itself proved that he was weak, that a stronger man would have moved past it by now. This belief deepened his helplessness, and he began to avoid any situation that might remind him of that day. He stopped walking past the demolition site where it happened, taking a longer route to work. He avoided the section of the hardware store where the jackhammers were kept, and he stopped talking to Carlos’s widow, even though she had called him several times. On the job, he stopped volunteering for any task that involved climbing or working near unstable structures, which made him look unreliable to his crew. His foreman noticed that Joe was no longer the steady, dependable worker he had been, and Joe was certain that people thought less of him, which only confirmed his belief that he was inadequate.

What finally brought Joe to therapy was a moment of near-panic on a new construction site. A forklift dropped a pallet of bricks a little too hard, and the sound—the crack and the dust—sent Joe into a spiral of intrusive images and smells that left him shaking in his truck for twenty minutes afterward. His foreman told him to get help or find another job. Joe is terrified that if he starts talking about what happened, he will fall apart completely, that the memories will swallow him whole. But he is even more afraid of losing the only job he has, of proving to everyone that he really is as broken as he feels. He hopes that therapy can help him forget, though a part of him already knows that forgetting is not what he needs.
